title: SGLT2 Inhibitors and Euglycemic DKA
bottomLine: SGLT2-associated DKA can occur with glucose that looks only mildly elevated. In a client taking an SGLT2 inhibitor, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachypnea, dehydration, ketones or unexplained acidosis require DKA assessment regardless of the glucose number.
recognize: Risk rises with fasting, illness, dehydration, surgery or insulin deficiency
differentiate: HHS has profound hyperosmolality/dehydration and usually much higher glucose with little ketoacidosis
Simple gastroenteritis does not explain metabolic acidosis and ketones in this risk context
assessment: Last SGLT2 dose and insulin exposure
workup: Bicarbonate, anion gap and blood gas
management: Temporarily hold SGLT2 inhibitor when ordered
medicationSafety: Diabetes Canada recommends temporary withholding during acute severe illness/dehydration and around major surgery
Do not reassure based on glucose alone
counselling: Seek urgent care for ketone/acidosis symptoms
followUp: Medication restart only after clinical review
examTrap: Ruling out DKA because glucose is only 10–12 mmol/L.
oneLinePearl: On an SGLT2 inhibitor, sick + ketones beats the glucose number.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada pharmacologic glycemic management guidance

title: Methimazole Safety
bottomLine: Fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers while taking methimazole can signal agranulocytosis; jaundice, dark urine or RUQ pain can signal hepatic injury. Treat these as urgent medication-toxicity assessments, not routine side effects.
differentiate: A viral sore throat cannot be safely assumed until neutropenia is considered
Thyroid storm is hypermetabolic instability rather than drug-induced neutropenia
management: Hold/discontinue according to the medical plan when serious toxicity suspected
medicationSafety: Agranulocytosis is rare but potentially fatal
Do not normalize fever and sore throat without assessment
counselling: Report fever, sore throat or jaundice immediately
followUp: Alternative thyroid treatment and laboratory follow-up as directed
examTrap: Offering routine cold care for fever and sore throat without considering agranulocytosis.
oneLinePearl: Methimazole + fever/sore throat = CBC thinking now.

title: Levothyroxine Safety
bottomLine: Levothyroxine requires consistent administration and awareness of absorption interactions such as calcium and iron. Palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, angina or atrial dysrhythmia after dose changes suggest over-replacement and require assessment.
recognize: Under-replacement: fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation
Over-replacement: tachycardia, tremor, heat intolerance and insomnia
Variable control with inconsistent timing or interacting supplements
differentiate: Thyroid symptoms overlap with anxiety and cardiac disease, so use clinical context and thyroid testing
management: Separate interacting supplements/medications according to pharmacy guidance
Adjust dose only through the prescriber plan
medicationSafety: Do not independently double or alter doses
Older adults and people with cardiac disease may require cautious titration
counselling: Keep lab follow-up after dose or formulation changes
examTrap: Giving calcium or iron at the same time as levothyroxine without checking spacing instructions.
oneLinePearl: Levothyroxine likes consistency and distance from absorption blockers.

title: Chronic Corticosteroid Safety
bottomLine: Long-term systemic steroids suppress the HPA axis and raise infection, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, skin and muscle risks. Never advise abrupt cessation; vomiting or illness with missed steroids plus hypotension, profound weakness, confusion or hypoglycemia can indicate adrenal crisis.
recognize: Hyperglycemia, skin fragility and proximal weakness
Infection may present with blunted inflammatory signs
Adrenal symptoms after abrupt interruption or major stress
differentiate: Chronic steroid adverse effects are different from acute adrenal crisis with shock/weakness/GI symptoms
workup: Glucose and infection studies as indicated
management: Use stress-dose therapy when ordered for at-risk clients
medicationSafety: Abrupt withdrawal after chronic exposure can be dangerous
Immunosuppressive dosing may affect infection and vaccine planning
examTrap: Stopping long-term prednisone abruptly because the original condition is improved.
oneLinePearl: Chronic steroids must taper; stress plus missed doses can crash cortisol.

title: Metformin Acute-Illness and Renal Safety
bottomLine: Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia by itself, but severe renal dysfunction, hypoperfusion, hypoxia, dehydration or major acute illness increase lactic-acidosis risk. During dehydrating illness or AKI risk, verify sick-day hold instructions; contrast decisions depend on renal function and local guidance rather than a universal rule.
recognize: Acute dehydration or reduced intake in a metformin user
Possible lactic acidosis: profound weakness, tachypnea, GI symptoms or hypotension
differentiate: Routine metformin GI upset does not explain shock or severe acidosis
management: Temporarily hold during dehydrating/AKI-risk illness when directed by sick-day plan
Treat shock, hypoxia, dehydration or renal injury
medicationSafety: Diabetes Canada identifies metformin among drugs temporarily withheld during acute illness with dehydration/AKI risk
Do not restart after severe AKI until clinically reviewed
counselling: Seek care for persistent vomiting, dehydration or severe weakness
followUp: Confirm renal recovery and safe medication restart
examTrap: Automatically continuing metformin through shock/AKI—or automatically stopping it for every contrast study regardless of renal function and policy.
oneLinePearl: Metformin safety follows kidneys and perfusion, not a one-size-fits-all rule.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada pharmacologic glycemic management guidance
